blocks.text: Both heat and work correspond to the transfer of energy by some means. The idea was first applied to the steam engine, where it was natural to transfer heat in and get work out; consequently it made sense to define both heat in and work out as positive quantities. Hence work done by the system on its environment is considered positive, while work done on the system by the environment is taken as negative. If an amount of heat Q enters the system, it could manifest itself either as an increase in internal energy or as a resulting quantity of work performed by the system on the surroundings, or both.

Work can be expressed in terms of directly measurable variables. Consider a gas enclosed in a cylinder with a movable, frictionless piston of cross-sectional area A (Fig. 6.4a). In equilibrium the system occupies volume V and exerts a pressure P on the walls of the cylinder and its piston; the force F exerted by the gas on the piston is PA. Assume the gas expands through delta V very slowly, so that it remains in equilibrium (Fig. 6.4b). As the piston moves up through a small distance delta y, the work W done by the gas is W = F delta y = P A delta y. Since A delta y = delta V (change in volume), W = P delta V ... (6.4). The work done can also be calculated from the area under the curve of the P-V graph (Fig. 6.5). Knowing the details of the change in internal energy and the mechanical work done, we are in a position to describe the general principles which deal with heat energy and its transformation into mechanical energy: the laws of thermodynamics.

blocks.alt: (a) A cylinder holding gas of pressure P and volume V, closed by a piston of area A; a downward force F acts on the piston rod. (b) The same cylinder standing on a hot plate: the piston has risen through delta y, shown between two dashed lines, and the gas now has volume V + delta V.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.4: A gas is sealed in a cylinder by a weightless, frictionless piston. The constant downward applied force F equals PA, and when the piston is displaced, downward work is done on the gas (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.4).

blocks.alt: A P-V graph with origin 0. A dashed line from P on the vertical axis leads to B. A magenta line with an arrow runs from B to C at constant pressure, labelled Constant pressure. The rectangle ABCD down to the V axis, between V1 at A and V2 at D, is shaded, with a dashed double arrow delta V across it.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.5: Work done as the area under the P-V graph at constant pressure (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.5).
